exercises.label: Exercise 15.B1 — Medium: Reverify after the input envelope changes
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The answer determines the first unit stays active, identifies the only remaining breakpoint, simplifies both affine branches, evaluates their endpoint ranges and names the attained global extrema. It applies the exact0.3 maximum to59.7 and explicitly treats equality, zero margin, the changed negative minimum and the excluded residual. The claimed deterministic range is justified by exhaustive branches rather than sampled endpoints.
exercises.replacement_html:
1. Determine which ReLUs can change status. The correction is $n(z)=\operatorname{ReLU}(z+0.2)-2\operatorname{ReLU}(z-0.1)$. On the new interval $[-0.1,0.5]$, $z+0.2\ge0.1\gt0$, so the first unit is active everywhere. The second changes status only at $z=0.1$.

2. Optimize each affine branch. For $-0.1\le z\le0.1$, the second output is zero and $n(z)=z+0.2$, increasing from $0.1$ to $0.3$ degrees. For $0.1\le z\le0.5$, both units are active and $n(z)=z+0.2-2(z-0.1)=0.4-z$, decreasing from $0.3$ to $-0.1$ degrees. The maximum $0.3$ is attained at $z=0.1$, and the minimum $-0.1$ at $z=0.5$. The two continuous branches therefore give exact range $[-0.1,0.3]$.

3. Apply the specified upper limit. The worst modeled temperature is $59.7+0.3=60.0$ degrees, so every allowed feature satisfies the stated non-strict $\le60$ limit. The certificate has zero margin. A strict-separation requirement or an additional positive implementation/model error would need a new allowance. The old correction minimum zero cannot be reused after the input domain changes, and the additional calibrated residual was explicitly excluded from this exercise.

exercises.label: Exercise 15.B2 — Hard: Calibrate a whole ten-step forecast
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The solution explains the integer-ceiling condition, rearranges the0.99(n+1) requirement to n≥99, and checks the boundary order statistic. It defines calibration objects as whole trajectories and connects the max-score event to all ten residual bounds, then adds both neural and residual allowances to59.35 and states the0.03 margin. It correctly limits coverage to a marginal exchangeability guarantee and contrasts it with the0.90 pointwise union bound.
exercises.replacement_html:
1. Find when a finite order statistic is available. The calibration index is $k=\lceil0.99(n+1)\rceil$. Because $n$ is an integer, $k\le n$ holds exactly when $0.99(n+1)\le n$. Rearranging gives $0.99\le0.01n$, hence $n\ge99$. At the smallest size $n=99$, $k=\lceil99\rceil=99$, the largest calibration trajectory score. Smaller samples require the conservative infinite-threshold convention.

2. Translate the score event into a joint residual bound. Each calibration example is a complete ten-step trajectory, scored by $s=\max_{1\le t\le10}|r_t|$. Thus $s\le0.32$ is exactly the event that every one of the ten residual magnitudes is at most $0.32$ degrees. Under exchangeability of the $99$ calibration trajectories together with the next trajectory, split conformal gives this one event marginal probability at least $99/100=0.99$.

3. Test all ten temperatures on that event. At each step the nominal value is $59.35$, the neural correction is at most $0.3$, and the residual is at most $0.32$. Therefore $T_t\le59.35+0.3+0.32=59.97\le60$ degrees for every $t=1,\ldots,10$, leaving $0.03$ degrees of margin. The proposal passes the modeled inequality throughout the forecast on the joint residual-coverage event.

This is marginal coverage over calibration and new-trajectory randomness, not a deterministic promise about every future trajectory or a conditional guarantee at every selected input. Ten separate 99 percent pointwise statements would, by a union bound alone, give only $1-10(0.01)=0.90$ joint coverage. Scoring the whole trajectory directly changes the calibration object and supplies the requested joint event.

exercises.label: Easy 1 — Turn a label claim into a scalar specification
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: The correct current answer compresses the logit subtraction and monotonicity into p=1−3x, and gives logits(1,2) without their forward substitutions. Expand the scalar violation construction, endpoint/worst-case calculation, tie threshold and actual counterexample; keep the distinction between a positive sound upper bound and proof of failure.
exercises.replacement_html:
Write the requested strict comparison for every allowed input. Class1 must beat class2 throughout$D=[0,1]$, meaning $f_1(x)\gt f_2(x)$ for every$x\in D$. Define the scalar violation objective as the competitor minus the desired class:

$$\begin{aligned} p(x)&=f_2(x)-f_1(x)\\ &=(-x+2)-(2x+1)\\ &=-x+2-2x-1=1-3x. \end{aligned}$$

The desired property is$p(x)\lt0$ everywhere, equivalently$\max_{x\in[0,1]}p(x)\lt0$. A non-strict inequality would allow tied logits and would express a different requirement.

Find the exact worst case. The affine slope is$-3$, so$p$ decreases as$x$ increases. Its endpoint values are$p(0)=1$ and$p(1)=1-3=-2$. Therefore the largest violation is

$$p^*=\max_{x\in[0,1]}(1-3x)=1,\qquad x^*=0.$$

The strict specification fails. The tie occurs when$1-3x=0$, or$x=1/3$: class2 wins for$x\lt1/3$, the logits tie at$1/3$, and class1 wins for$x\gt1/3$.

Forward-check a counterexample. At$x=0$, $f_1(0)=2(0)+1=1$ and$f_2(0)=-0+2=2$. Thus class2 strictly wins at an allowed input. This concrete evaluation proves failure independently of a relaxation.

Interpret the incomplete verifier's upper bound in the correct direction. A sound upper bound$\bar p=1.4$ says only$p^*\le1.4$. That statement allows either a positive or a negative true maximum, so it does not alone prove failure. A sound bound below zero would certify the desired strict comparison; a nonnegative bound leaves it unresolved unless another argument is available. Here the actual counterexample$x=0$ and exact maximum1 supply that argument. At a zero gap, label behavior also depends on a specified tie rule, whereas this question explicitly requires strict winning.
